title: Peruvian Pepper: Ancient Peruvian Peppers You Can Visit
meta_description: The pink peppercorns in an expensive grinder come from this Andean tree, not pepper at all. Three mapped, in Barcelona, Melbourne and Setubal.
intro: The pink peppercorns sold in an expensive pepper grinder are not pepper. They come from this tree, an Andean member of the cashew family with no botanical relation to black pepper, carried out of South America by Spanish colonial trade in the sixteenth century and planted everywhere the climate allowed. Its weeping grey-green foliage moves in any wind at all, and a crushed leaf smells sharply of pepper, the family trait that earned it the name. In Melbourne it became the tree of colonial Australia, planted by the thousand along stock routes and rail sidings because it shrugged off drought and neglect; the one mapped here, in Richmond's Madden Grove, stands on ground set aside as a survey paddock in 1836, one of the city's earliest public reservations. Barcelona and Setubal took the opposite path, planting it singly as an ornamental curiosity, the softest tree in each garden it stands in.
